name: Bias in Tech Forecasting
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Why Every Forecast Misses in the Same Direction
lesson.summary: Sunk cost, optimism, survivorship, and narrative biases are not separate curiosities, they are specific instances of a broader, well documented pattern in technology forecasting: overestimating short-term impact while underestimating or mis-timing long-term impact.
lesson.body:
The previous several chapters covered four distinct cognitive biases, sunk cost, optimism, survivorship, and narrative, each explained largely on its own terms. Viewed together, they are not a random assortment. They are specific mechanisms behind a much broader and frequently observed pattern that shows up specifically in how societies forecast the impact of new technologies, and naming that broader pattern makes the individual pieces easier to recognize when they appear together.

The clearest statement of this broader pattern is often attributed to the futurist Roy Amara, sometimes referred to as Amara's Law: we tend to overestimate the effect of a technology in the short run, and underestimate its effect in the long run. It is worth treating this as a useful heuristic generalization rather than a rigid, physics-like law, but it captures something genuinely and repeatedly observed across many technologies, an initial burst of overexcited short-term prediction, followed eventually, for the technologies that do pan out, by a longer-term impact that actually exceeds what even the early boosters claimed, just arriving on a much longer timeline than promised.

A related and more popularized version of the same underlying shape is the Gartner Hype Cycle, an industry framework describing new technologies as passing through an initial peak of inflated expectations, followed by a trough of disillusionment as reality fails to match the early hype, and eventually, for technologies that mature successfully, a slope of enlightenment toward genuinely productive use. This framework is worth treating as a useful descriptive mental map rather than a rigorously validated predictive model, it was not derived from controlled experiments, but the general shape it describes echoes the same overestimate-short-run, underestimate-long-run dynamic that shows up in more careful research.

Applying this directly to quantum computing forecasting reveals a suspicious pattern once you look for it: predictions of practical, broadly useful quantum advantage have clustered around roughly five to ten years in the future for over two decades, essentially independent of what year the prediction was actually made. That specific pattern, a stable rough estimate that never seems to compress as time passes, is consistent with optimism bias operating persistently inside a forecasting community rather than a genuinely improving technical estimate. Meanwhile, press coverage tends to treat each new qubit count record as more significant than the underlying, much slower progress on error rates and error correction actually warrants, consistent with the narrative fallacy compressing a conditional technical result into an unconditional breakthrough story.

None of this points toward blanket cynicism about technology forecasts. Some technologies, electricity and the internet among them, really did eventually exceed even their most enthusiastic early boosters' claims, just over a much longer timeframe than anyone initially promised. The correct response is calibration rather than dismissal: treat technology forecasts, including confident ones from genuinely credentialed experts, as systematically biased in a known and fairly predictable direction, and adjust your own expectations accordingly, rather than either swallowing them whole or discounting them entirely.
